---
title: "Adjudicated Persistence, Generalization, Feedback, Continual Learning, and Unlearning"
unit_id: "unit-21"

## The Same Green Patch, Two Different Lessons

Continue the hypothetical repository story, not a reported learning trial.
The learner sees two patches that produce the same visible result.
Both repair a failing dependency upgrade. Both pass the test suite. Both are
merged after review. If learning means collecting successful examples, the two
events appear nearly interchangeable.

They are not.

The first patch succeeds because the maintainer remembers an undocumented
compatibility condition. The dependency may be upgraded only after a generated
schema has been rebuilt. The code change is routine; the missing knowledge is
the defect. A dated semantic-memory entry, linked to the affected package and
its source evidence, may be the smallest durable correction.

The second patch succeeds only after a reviewer notices that the tool used to
edit the manifest silently drops an optional field. The maintainer did not lack
knowledge. The tool violated its contract. Another memory entry would warn
future agents while leaving the faulty mechanism in place. A typed regression check can block the lossy transformation while the tool is
repaired or replaced. The check is not the repair itself; an admitted manual
route may carry the work until the corrected implementation is qualified.

Equal outcomes conceal unequal causes. A system that stores every success in
memory accumulates folklore. A system that retrains on every success changes
parameters when a test would have sufficed. A system that compiles every
repeated behavior into a procedure can preserve an accidental workaround. A
blanket refusal of updates can leave known correctable defects in place.
Correct restraint after one uninformative success remains a legitimate choice.

The question after an experience is therefore not simply, "What did we learn?"
It is a sequence of harder questions:

1. Did the outcome carry an informative lesson at all?
2. Which causal account of the outcome remains plausible?
3. What candidate change follows from that account?
4. Where could the change persist?
5. What is the least consequential locus that can solve the problem?
6. What evidence and authority does that commitment require?
7. How will the change be qualified, monitored, revised, and retired?

This sequence is the adaptive commit boundary. It separates experience from
durable structure. It is not a single omniscient controller. It is a governed
decision process whose records can be challenged and whose commitments carry
correction, retirement, and bounded recovery duties. Reversing one stored
artifact does not undo every consequence of its earlier use.

## An Outcome Is Not a Lesson

An outcome is an observation about what happened under particular conditions.
A lesson is a proposed regularity, cause, policy, or intervention inferred from
that observation. Confusing the two converts correlation into architecture.

A successful patch does not explain why it worked, whether it was necessary,
whether the test captured the objective, or whether it transfers. Failure may
reflect a constraint, outage, stale evaluator, permission problem or chance.
Reward and blame do not identify cause.

The experience record should preserve more than a scalar score. It needs the
decision context available at the time, alternatives that were eligible then,
the action taken, predictions, observed effects, evaluator identities,
interventions, confounders, residuals, and later corrections. Counterfactual
comparators must be decision-time fair. An alternative invented after seeing
the result cannot be presented as though the agent irrationally ignored it.

This record still does not make causal inference automatic. It keeps the
epistemic debt visible. A candidate lesson can say that the schema-ordering
explanation is supported by the event and by a reproduction. It cannot quietly
upgrade that statement to a universal dependency rule.

Predicted success may add confidence without justifying structural change;
failure may expose an inadequate account without identifying a remedy.
Rewarding visible updates favors activity over correction. Correct restraint
must remain an admissible decision.

## Candidate Lessons Need Identity

A candidate lesson should be an artifact, not an atmosphere. It needs a stable
identifier, proposition, scope, evidence lineage, causal alternatives,
assumptions, affected surfaces, expected benefit, possible harm, expiry or
review condition, and named owner.

For the first patch, a candidate might be:

> Within repository family R and dependency line D, regenerate schema S before
> accepting an upgrade candidate, because the generated interface changes the
> compatibility test.

Its bounded population and causal hypothesis link to the incident,
reproduction, dissent and next review date.

The second patch yields a different candidate:

> Tool T must preserve optional manifest field F under a parse-write round trip;
> reject its output when the field is lost.

That lesson points toward executable enforcement, not recollection. Its natural
qualification includes a failing regression before the repair, a passing
regression after it, and checks that the accepted field-preservation rule has
the intended scope. One passing case does not qualify every transformation.

Explicit identity permits later revision, multiple lessons per incident and
one lesson across incidents without merging histories. Conflicting candidates
can coexist during adjudication.

The identity should survive realization. If the schema-ordering lesson becomes
a memory entry, a checklist item, and eventually a tool precondition, each
artifact should point back to the candidate and to the decision that authorized
its form. Otherwise descendants become orphaned folklore that cannot be
reliably withdrawn.

## The Adaptive Commit Boundary

::: {#adaptive-commit-text}
**Text version.** Experience may justify proposing a candidate lesson. Scoped
adjudication checks whether learning is eligible, the causal account is
adequate, the persistence locus fits, the commitment is proportionate, and
lifecycle custody is available. A candidate can be deferred, rejected, or sent
for more evidence. An admitted candidate still needs the qualifications for
its chosen surface and a current commit grant before durable change. The
result retains its scope and review or revocation route. This is a proposed
decision structure; a successful patch neither proves the lesson nor permits
it to rewrite the evaluator that will judge later changes.
:::

::: {.asi-reader-diagram tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Scrollable adaptive commit decision" aria-describedby="adaptive-commit-text" style="--asi-diagram-width: 38rem;"}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Experience is not an automatic durable update
  accDescr: Experience can produce a candidate lesson. A scoped adjudication checks eligibility, causal adequacy, locus, proportionality, and lifecycle custody. It may defer, reject, or request evidence. If admitted, a qualified change at the chosen locus needs a commit grant before it becomes durable. The committed change retains its scope, review, and revocation route; it cannot ratify itself.
  E["Experience"] --> L["Candidate lesson"]
  L --> A{"Scoped adjudication"}
  A -- "not ready" --> D["Defer, reject, or seek evidence"]
  A -- "admit candidate" --> Q["Qualified change at chosen locus"]
  Q --> G{"Commit grant current?"}
  G -- "no" --> D
  G -- "yes" --> C["Scoped durable change"]
```

:::

*Figure. A lesson and a durable change are different objects. Qualification
and a current commit grant stand between them.*

Scroll inside the frame when needed; the complete text version is above.


The adaptive commit boundary receives experience and candidate lessons, then
decides whether any durable change is warranted. Its output is not merely
"learn" or "do not learn." It can reject, defer, request evidence, choose a
locus, limit scope, stage a canary, require human approval, create a temporary
lease, or record an unresolved residual.

The decision should answer five tests.

**Learning eligibility.** Is there a material mismatch, opportunity, or newly
supported regularity? Is the feedback admissible? Are obvious evaluator,
provenance, and tampering failures excluded?

**Causal adequacy.** Does the proposed change address the plausible cause rather
than merely correlate with the outcome? What alternatives remain live?

**Locus fit.** Which persistence surface changes the right behavior with the
least unrelated effect?

**Commitment proportionality.** Is the evidence strong enough for the cost,
reach, duration, and reversibility of the proposed change?

**Lifecycle custody.** Can the system qualify, observe, revoke, and account for
the change and its descendants?

These tests need not be administered by one service. A local tool owner may
approve a test fix. A memory service may accept a short-lived note under a
standing policy. A parameter update may require an independent evaluator and a
deployment authority. The boundary is architectural: no consequential
persistence surface should be writable merely because an upstream component
produced a high score.

Centralizing every decision would create cost, latency, and a new target for
capture. The practical design is federated adjudication under shared contracts.
Local authorities can act within explicit scopes; expensive review is reserved
for high-commitment or cross-surface changes. Each route retains enough permitted evidence for its declared reconstruction
claim, recording missingness and retention limits. An existing update policy
can grant a bounded commit; this need not become a new human approval for every
memory write or training step.

## A Good Idea Can Be the Wrong Default

A reusable abstraction can be true, elegant, and well verified without
deserving automatic use. Perhaps the ordinary solver already finds every
answer. Perhaps retrieval costs more than it saves. Perhaps the abstraction
helps one family and distracts another. The persistence decision needs a field
for semantic validity and a different field for measured future benefit.

That measurement also needs its own round. Candidates are extracted and
checked during development; the library is frozen; held-out tasks are then run
with absence, placebo, and removal controls. A successful candidate enters the
next version, not the version it was tested against. Otherwise the test set
quietly becomes training data and the system certifies a moving target.

This separation allows a humane outcome for uncertain knowledge. A candidate
can remain archived, inspectable, and available to specialists without being
routed as a default. Denial of promotion is not deletion of the idea. It is a
claim about the evidence for this use, distribution, search method, and budget.

## Eight Places a Lesson Can Live

Learning discussions often jump from experience directly to parameter update.
An engineered system has more choices.

### Context

The lightest intervention is to supply information during the current task.
Context is appropriate when the need is temporary, local, or not yet supported
for reuse. Its mounted use ends with the context lease, while stored copies
need their own disposition. Repeated retrieval costs attention and can fail
under context pressure.

### Semantic Memory

Memory preserves a proposition across tasks. It is useful when later decisions
need dated, challengeable knowledge. Memory writes should retain provenance,
scope, confidence, conflicts, review conditions, and deletion obligations.
Memory can be corrected more directly than parameters, but stale or
overgeneralized entries can influence many actions invisibly.

### Procedure

A procedure preserves an ordered method: checks, branches, stop conditions,
and recovery. It fits recurrent work whose control flow is understood.
Procedural memory saves reasoning effort but can harden yesterday's workaround
into tomorrow's default.

### Tool or Test

A tool changes what actions are possible; a test changes what artifacts may
pass. These are strong loci when the lesson describes a machine-checkable
invariant. They provide direct feedback and often precise rollback. They can
also encode a mistaken rule with high authority.

### Model Parameters

Parameter changes can alter broad behavior where explicit rules or retrieval
are inadequate. Their reach is also their danger. The changed knowledge may be
hard to locate, explain, delete, or reverse without collateral effects. A
parameter update requires evidence beyond the convenience of having a training
pipeline.

### Evaluator

Sometimes the failure is not generation but judgment. An evaluator may need new
tests, examples, calibrations, independence rules, or adversarial probes.
Changing the evaluator changes what future learning optimizes, so it cannot be
treated as neutral maintenance.

### Environment

The best lesson may be to change the world around the agent: repair an API,
remove an ambiguous interface, restrict an unsafe capability, improve
observability, or redesign a workflow. Agent adaptation should not compensate
forever for a defective environment.

### Institution

Organizations learn through roles, permissions, review duties, escalation
rules, incentives, and norms. Institutional change is appropriate when the
defect arises from coordination or authority. It is costly, politically
consequential, and difficult to reverse, so technical convenience cannot be its
only justification.

Combining loci creates adaptation debt unless their authority order,
carrying cost and retirement are explicit. A temporary reminder may support a
tool repair, then expire when the test replaces it.

## Locus Is Part of the Claim

A lesson cannot be evaluated apart from where it will live. "The agent should
check generated schemas" means something different as advice in context, a
retrieved memory, a mandatory procedure step, a blocking test, or a learned
parameter tendency. The proposition may be similar while its reliability,
reach, and authority change.

Adjudication selects an intervention, not just a true sentence. An accurate
causal account can yield a bad placement: a parameter update may improve the
average while missing the critical boundary; a blocking test may enforce the
rule but reject legitimate cases outside its scope.

The system should make cross-locus alternatives explicit. For each candidate it
can ask:

- How often will the lesson be needed, and how costly is retrieval failure?
- Does the lesson have crisp preconditions and a machine-checkable consequence?
- Must it change generation, judgment, permission, or the environment itself?
- Who is affected if the lesson is wrong?
- Can its active effect and descendants be found later?
- What evidence would justify moving it to a stronger or broader locus?

A hybrid can be justified: temporary memory protects work during a tool
repair, a canary gathers independent evidence, or an institutional rule
requires a test without prescribing implementation. Each combination needs
an authority order and retirement plan.

Conflicts between loci are normal. Memory may recommend an action that a newer
tool contract forbids. A learned policy may bypass a procedure. An evaluator
may reward behavior that an institutional rule prohibits. The stack needs a
typed resolution order: constitutional and authority constraints bound action;
current executable contracts govern their surfaces; qualified procedures and
memories advise within those bounds; parameter behavior remains subject to all
of them. That order is itself a governed policy, not a claim that higher layers
are always correct.

Conflict records are learning evidence. Repeated disagreement between a policy
and a tool precondition may reveal stale parameters, a bad precondition, or a
shift in the environment. Silently choosing one side destroys the signal that
could correct either.

## Minimum Sufficient Persistence

The default should be the least persistent, least expansive intervention that
meets the need under the required reliability.

"Least" does not mean weakest. A tool invariant can be more decisive and less
wide-ranging than a parameter update. A narrow institutional permission change
can be safer than asking every agent to remember a policy in context. The
comparison must include reach, duration, reversibility, observability,
qualification cost, deletion cost, and expected collateral effect.

For each candidate locus, the adjudicator can estimate a commitment profile:

| Dimension | Lower commitment | Higher commitment |
|---|---|---|
| Reach | one task or repository | many domains or organizations |
| Duration | one lease | indefinite default |
| Reversibility | direct removal | diffuse descendants |
| Observability | explicit artifact | latent behavior |
| Authority | advisory | blocks or initiates action |
| Coupling | isolated surface | changes evaluators and learners |
| Removal target | one stored object | learned influence or prior effects |

The profile informs the evidence burden. Profiles may be incomparable: one
route is shorter-lived but harder to observe, while another is explicit but
more widely enforced. A declared consumer policy chooses among qualified
examined alternatives; the profile does not prove a universal minimum. One reproducible incident may
justify a scoped test for the exact failure. It should not justify a universal
parameter update. A broad update may eventually be warranted, but only after
holdouts, competing explanations, transfer tests, rollback rehearsals, and
independent review appropriate to its reach.

The system should also price not changing. A narrow memory entry that is easy to
revoke but too unreliable for a safety-critical precondition may be false
economy. Minimum sufficient persistence minimizes whole-lifecycle loss, not the
number of artifacts created today.

## Generalization Is a Prospective Claim

A lesson becomes more consequential when it claims to transfer beyond the
events that produced it. Generalization is not a feeling that the rule is
"fundamental." It is a forecast over a named population under stated
conditions.

The schema-ordering lesson might forecast success across repositories using the
same generator and dependency family. It should name exclusions, expected
failure modes, metrics, evaluation window, and what counts as a meaningful
miss. New repositories become prospective tests rather than post hoc anecdotes.

Transfer asks whether the intervention remains useful under changed task,
domain, model, organization, or execution environment. Scaling asks how its
behavior changes with data, model capacity, compute, agent population, or
deployment reach. These are distinct claims. A method can generalize within one
distribution yet fail under scale because coordination or evaluator pressure
changes.

Forecasts should be registered before outcomes are known. Repairs remain in the
record. Failed forecasts are not deleted when a later version succeeds.
Material changes in the learner, data, evaluator, or environment invalidate old
qualification unless a prospective rule says otherwise.

Recording failed forecasts prevents a favorable anecdote from becoming a
general principle immune to counterevidence.

Generalization evidence should travel with the realized lesson. A memory entry
may be valid for dependency line D but not its successor. A procedure may have
been qualified with one tool version. A parameter checkpoint may have passed
one distribution and failed another. Consumers need those boundaries at use
time, not only in an archived experiment report.

Representation convergence needs an equally specific claim. The
[2026 JEPA/Platonic Representation paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39302v1)
proves a conditional population result for a finite world with injective
renderings, matched positive pairs and marginals, and an identity predictor.
Its empirical models do not satisfy every theorem assumption. Similar latent
geometry therefore supplies neither a generalization guarantee nor evidence
that the representation supports a new causal intervention. Unit 11 owns the
grounding question; this chapter keeps theorem conditions separate from a
forecast about the next task. The external Platonic Representation Hypothesis
also remains distinct from our proposed Platonic World Model's semantic
governance contracts.

## Feedback Is Evidence, Not an Objective

Feedback can come from users, reviewers, automated tests, reward models,
environmental outcomes, affected parties, or the system's own monitors. Each
source observes part of the world through incentives and failure modes.

A thumbs-up may reflect politeness or persuasion. A test may miss the user's
objective; a reward model may reproduce annotator bias; an engagement metric
may improve while autonomy or trust deteriorate.

Feedback admission records the source, observable scope, selection,
incentives, candidate influence and intended target. Conflicting feedback
remains visible.

Two of our proposals make that admission boundary more concrete. The
[Regret Engine](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/policy-optimization-and-learning-from-feedback.html#regret-packets-are-protected-feedback-not-actor-rewards)
joins the decision-time record, actual outcome, feasible comparators and
uncertain counterfactuals in a Regret Packet. Incident severity, causal
contribution and eligibility for learning remain different judgements. The
actor cannot be the sole judge of its own comparator set, causal blame or
eligibility for an update. A diagnostic packet is not automatically a reward.

[Assurance-Shift Learning](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/data-engines-continual-learning-and-unlearning.html#regret-aware-replay-without-failure-fixation)
then asks which exceptions still teach a mature learner. Its replay retains
protected successful cases and a counterexample to an overbroad repair, while
keeping natural prevalence separate from diagnostic probes. Negative priority
can decay when the named learner, repair and regression evidence justify it;
elapsed time alone does not retire the lesson. A changed learner or operating
region can reactivate the bundle. These are proposed feedback and replay
contracts, not measured learning gains, parameter unlearning or privacy erasure.

Optimization begins only after this epistemic work, and it must preserve the
difference between proxy and target. Improving a reward is evidence about the
optimization process. It is not proof that the underlying objective improved.

This is the anti-Goodhart boundary. A candidate policy needs target evaluations
outside the reward used to produce it, held-out cases, contamination checks,
reward-hacking probes, regression checks, authority review, and a rollback
route. The stronger the optimization pressure, the less safe it is to infer
target quality from proxy movement alone.

Human feedback does not dissolve the problem. People can be inconsistent,
fatigued, manipulated, strategically selective, or unable to inspect the
relevant process. A persuasive system may improve its approval rate by changing
the approver rather than the result. High-stakes feedback therefore needs
independent channels, protected dissent, sampling of affected parties, and
limits on the candidate's access to the evaluation process.

## Policy Updates Are Leased Candidates

A policy update should enter operation through a lease, not a coronation. The
lease names the candidate identity, training process, eligible feedback,
baseline, target and proxy metrics, holdouts, contamination checks, authority
scope, canary population, stop conditions, residuals, rollback artifact, and
expiry.

The policy first runs in a shadow or bounded canary where its effects can be
compared with a competent baseline. It cannot expand its own authority. The
component that generated the update should not be the sole component that
qualifies it. Unexpected reward-target divergence, forgetting, evaluator
tampering, or rollback failure blocks promotion.

Successful canary operation is still local evidence. It does not prove broad
generalization or causal improvement. The candidate may have benefited from a
favorable sample, a changed workload, or hidden assistance. Promotion requires
the level of causal and transfer evidence appropriate to the next scope.

Rollback also needs a precise meaning. Restoring a policy artifact while
leaving changed memories, caches, tools, downstream data, or user effects is not
full reversal. The lease should declare which surfaces it can restore and which
residuals require separate custody.

The same discipline applies whether the update uses reinforcement learning,
preference optimization, supervised fine-tuning, evolutionary search, prompt
optimization, or a hand-edited routing table. Optimization family does not
waive governance.

## Continual Learning Is State Management

Continual learning asks a system to acquire useful behavior while retaining,
revising, or discarding earlier behavior over time. That makes it a state-
management problem before it is an algorithm contest.

The learner must know what changed, from which data and feedback, under which
contract, with which expected interactions. It needs baselines for retained
capabilities, prospective measures of new capability, and tests for interference.
Without them, "continual" can mean an unversioned stream of updates whose
failures appear only after old tasks disappear from view.

The stability-plasticity tradeoff is architectural. Excessive stability
preserves defects and blocks adaptation. Excessive plasticity overwrites useful
behavior and creates oscillation. Different persistence loci offer different
tradeoffs. Semantic memory can add dated knowledge without modifying shared model
weights. Procedures can isolate repeated methods. Parameters can integrate
patterns that explicit artifacts cannot capture, at the cost of harder
attribution and removal.

Replay buffers, retained examples, synthetic data, regularization, modular
adapters, and parameter isolation are mechanisms, not complete governance.
Their data rights, provenance, representativeness, contamination, and deletion
obligations remain live. A replay strategy can preserve performance by
preserving data that should no longer be retained.

Updates should preserve the state and history required by their advertised
recovery claim. An object version, bounded event log, or scheduled checkpoint
may suffice; a complete model copy after every gradient step is not required. Weights alone may omit optimizer, sampler, random-number,
curriculum, memory, evaluator, and descendant state. A learner cannot claim to
have returned to an earlier state if only one surface moved backward.

The [Memory-Centric Continual Learning survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29357v1)
sharpens this distinction. Updating what memory contains is different from
learning a new policy for writing, retrieving or forgetting it. A fixed
policy can store the schema-ordering episode and change the next answer while
the shared model weights remain fixed. If both content and selector change,
a better answer alone cannot identify the contribution of either one.
Retention under interference, adaptation and held-out transfer therefore need
separate checks, including matched stateful/reset and full-history or static
retrieval controls. More stored episodes or better retrieval scores do not
settle those behavioral questions. Nor do model-internal update frequencies,
discussed in Unit 19, assign the authority of the institutional clocks below.

## Multiple Update Clocks

Not every lesson should move at the same speed. An operational incident may
require a context warning in minutes, a memory correction in hours, a tool
repair in days, and a parameter update only after a qualified campaign. Forcing
all learning through one clock either delays urgent containment or grants
durable change on emergency evidence.

A practical stack separates at least three clocks.

The **fast clock** contains immediate risk. It can change context, quarantine an
artifact, disable a route, or attach a temporary warning under narrow standing
authority. Its leases are short and its non-claims explicit.

The **operational clock** turns repeated, reproduced lessons into memory,
procedures, tools, tests, or bounded policy canaries. It requires stronger
causal and qualification records and names a rollback owner.

The **structural clock** changes parameters, evaluators, environments, or
institutions whose effects are broad or difficult to reverse. It demands
independent evidence, competing baselines, transfer testing, descendant
planning, and authority commensurate with the commitment.

Evidence can move between clocks, but authority does not flow automatically. A
temporary quarantine can motivate a permanent control; it cannot authorize one.
Conversely, a slow structural review should not erase the operational fact that
a route is presently dangerous.

The clocks also limit oscillation. If every user complaint updates the policy
immediately, the system can chase noise or coordinated manipulation. If all
feedback waits for a quarterly retraining cycle, defects persist and affected
people have no timely remedy. Aggregation windows, rate limits, diversity
requirements, and change budgets belong to the learning contract.

Urgency itself is evidence that can be gamed. A candidate system might frame a
preferred update as emergency containment. Fast-clock changes therefore need
scope limits, automatic expiry, retrospective review, and a prohibition on
quietly becoming training labels or permanent policy.

These clocks connect continual learning to incident command and governance.
They let the system respond quickly without pretending that speed supplies
truth.

## Data Engines Carry Learning Obligations

A data engine turns observations, documents, demonstrations, labels, feedback,
and synthetic material into governed learning inputs. Its purpose is not merely
throughput. It preserves identity and obligations across acquisition,
transformation, selection, use, retention, and removal.

Each item needs source, rights, consent where applicable, time, population,
transformations, confidence, split eligibility, contamination status, derived
artifacts, retention policy, and deletion route. Batches and curricula need
reconstructible selection and order. Failed filters and excluded populations
belong in the record because they shape what the learner could discover.

Derived data complicates custody. One incident can produce a summary, embedding,
label, replay example, synthetic variant, evaluation case, and parameter update.
A later correction must address every known descendant carrying the defect or
obligation and record the discovery gap. A complete local inventory does not
prove that no unrecorded derivative exists. A flat list of training files is not enough.

The data engine should separate ingestion from admission. Availability does not
imply eligibility for training, evaluation, or memory. The same item may be
allowed for incident investigation and prohibited for parameter learning.
Rights and purpose can change, so admission decisions need version and expiry.

Synthetic data needs lineage to the models, prompts, tools, and source material
that generated it. High volume does not create independent evidence. Thousands
of variants from one mistaken premise remain one lineage with repeated error.

## The Data May Descend From the Policy

Continual learning becomes more dangerous when the current system helped
generate the next training set. A successful intervention can erase the event
it prevented. A recommender can alter exposure and preference. A classifier can
change which cases are reported or how categories are defined. Training on
those records without deployment ancestry teaches the successor an ambiguous
mixture of world change and model influence.

Every update therefore states the regime its evidence identifies. The data
engine records model versions, exposure, actions, measurement changes,
selection paths, and descendant summaries. It protects independent or
deliberately varied evidence where possible. When the effect cannot be
identified, the update carries an uncertainty range or residual rather than a
fictional clean target.

This is also a placement issue. Self-descended evidence may improve on-policy
behavior while weakening the system's ability to reason about alternatives.
The persistence adjudicator must count that lost counterfactual option as a
cost, not mistake adaptation to the created world for general learning.

## Unlearning Is Not One Claim

"The system forgot the data" can refer to several different outcomes:

1. the item is no longer returned through an access path;
2. the original and named derivatives are deleted from tracked storage;
3. a model no longer emits a target behavior under specified probes;
4. the item's measurable influence approaches an agreed retraining baseline;
5. membership or reconstruction risk falls under stated attacks;
6. downstream institutions and external copies have been notified or corrected.

None implies all the others.

Deleting a memory row can satisfy a local storage claim while leaving cached
retrievals, summaries, logs, backups, or parameter influence. Fine-tuning a
model to suppress an answer can change observed behavior without removing the
underlying influence or reducing privacy risk. Exact retraining without the
item is a useful comparator when feasible, but even it does not erase external
copies or effects already produced.

An unlearning request therefore needs a target, scope, threat model, descendant
graph, baseline, method, evaluation, residuals, and expiry. The result should
say exactly which claim was tested. "Removed from five tracked local storage
surfaces" is narrower and more useful than "forgotten."

Approximate unlearning requires competent attacks and utility tests. A method
can reduce one distance metric while worsening membership inference, or preserve
aggregate utility while damaging a small affected population. Results depend on
the model, data, attacker, and evaluation distribution. One score should not
collapse those axes.

Model-level guarantees can be stronger than a probe score. In
[Bourtoule et al., Definition III.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1912.03817v3),
unlearning compares the distribution from training and then removing the named
data with the distribution from the specified learning mechanism without that
data. Equality under that definition is a model-distribution claim, not a
promise that every related fact disappears from every output or external copy.

Suppose two independently admitted training records contain the same public
package-compatibility fact, and a removal request names one record. A reference
model trained without that record may still learn the fact from the other.
Continued output of the fact alone therefore cannot decide whether the named
record was removed or whether the updated model matches the reference. A
request forbidding every representation of the fact has a different target
and may put both records in scope. The target and admissible baseline must be
settled before interpreting a successful-looking suppression score.

In open deployment, inspecting tracked systems and bounded probes cannot
establish absence across unknown backups, recipients, or future access paths.
A mathematical guarantee quantifies over its stipulated mechanism and state;
it does not inventory unmodeled stores. Report the proved or tested claim,
assumptions, uncovered effects, and further-action owner separately.

## Scientific Discovery Is Governed Revision

Scientific learning is another persistence path. An observation becomes a
hypothesis; a hypothesis shapes an experiment; results may revise models,
procedures, tools, and institutions. The same adaptive boundary applies, with
additional pressure from researcher degrees of freedom.

A governed discovery campaign freezes the question, hypotheses, admissible
interventions, measurement plan, analysis, stopping rules, resource budget,
authority, and non-claims before confirmatory evidence is opened. Exploratory
work is welcome, but it remains labeled exploratory. Negative results, failed
attempts, protocol deviations, and discarded hypotheses stay in the record.

The experiment must distinguish observation from intervention and association
from causal identification. A result may support a local prediction without
discovering a general mechanism. Automated systems are especially capable of
generating many hypotheses and analyses, which increases both discovery
capacity and selection bias.

The boundary differs by activity. A laboratory agent executes physical
interventions; a computational agent produces code, experiments and papers;
a hypothesis system ranks explanations before testing. A robot command does
not supply an interpretation, a finished paper is not confirmation, and a
highly ranked hypothesis is not a discovery.

The larger the search, the more important its denominator becomes. Imagine a
system that generates ten thousand ideas, tests one hundred, repairs twenty
after seeing partial results, and publishes the single survivor. The survivor
may be valuable, but its history is part of the evidence. The discarded ideas,
failed code, abandoned experiments, pruning rules, compute allocation, and
human interventions cannot vanish merely because the final manuscript reads as
if one clean idea led to one clean test.

[Test-Time Memory Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32046v1) illustrates
how that history can itself become an adaptive resource. Its fixed-weight
model updates guidelines and source-case-linked strategies while retaining
archives, parent links and verifier results. A later proposal can use the
record of an earlier attempt without a weight update. Its five mathematical
construction tasks provide evidence about that search setting, not general
scientific discovery or held-out transfer. Reported method runtime excludes
candidate evaluation, and some TTT comparisons come from the original papers;
those distinctions matter when judging the apparent gain.

Our [Answerability Atlas synthesis](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/papers/answerability_atlas_synthesis.html)
shows a complementary discipline. Its positive development signal still
failed the declared advancement criteria, so confirmation was not run. A
later correction expanded the comparator pool on the same worlds and changed
the disposition from proceed to stop. That correction improves the account;
it is not independent confirmation, proof of zero effect, or permission to
reopen the closed controller line. Useful scientific memory must preserve
both the promising observation and the decision it actually justified.

Review has similar dependencies. Shared model families, training data,
retrieval, prompts and scoring habits limit independence. Related reviewers
can improve a draft, but their agreement is not independent confirmation.
Count the dependency graph, not the names.

Venue acceptance records one process's decision under its incentives and
attention limits, not a direct truth measurement. Automated publication also
consumes scarce reviewer attention, which belongs in the campaign cost.

Independent confirmation should not share every dependency with the discovery
path. New seeds on the same code and evaluator are useful, but they do not
provide the same evidence as a separately implemented replication. Material
changes after confirmation trigger readmission rather than inheriting the old
label.

Scientific conclusions remain versioned candidates. Later evidence can narrow,
supersede, or retire them without rewriting history. This is not a weakness of
the system. It is the mechanism by which correction remains possible.

## Adjudicating the Two Patches

Return to the two successful patches.

For the first, the system records the successful edit, the remembered schema
condition, and two alternatives: the dependency itself may be faulty, or the
test environment may contain a stale generated file. In this teaching case, matched clean runs vary regeneration order while
holding the named source, tool, and initial state fixed. They reproduce the
failure and repair within that scoped case, not across every repository.

The candidate lesson enters a short-lived semantic-memory locus. It is dated,
scoped to the dependency line, and linked to the reproduction. Why memory rather
than parameters? The proposition is explicit, narrow, and likely to change with
the next generator version. Why not a tool test immediately? Lack of upstream ownership does not rule out
a local guard. If a reliable preflight can enforce this scoped condition at
lower full cost, it should win. In this variant, the compatibility relation is
not yet exposed through a stable machine-readable check, and the permitted
workflow already includes maintainer review of the dated note. Memory is a
bounded aid to that review. If the task requires reliable automatic enforcement,
the note is insufficient: narrow or hold that use until an appropriate guard
is qualified.

The memory lease requires retrieval when dependency D is upgraded. Three later
upgrades become prospective transfer tests. Two support the rule; one reveals a
different generator path. The lesson narrows rather than counting the two wins
and hiding the miss.

When the tool owner adds an explicit precondition, the procedural checklist and
memory entry become redundant. The adjudicator retires the checklist, keeps the
memory as a historical explanation for one release cycle, then archives it from
active retrieval. Descendant links preserve the incident history without
continuing to spend attention.

For the second patch, the parse-write loss is reproduced directly. The
candidate lesson maps cleanly to a typed round-trip test. The test fails against
the old tool and passes after the repair. A canary checks representative
manifests, including ones without the optional field. The tool version and test
move together.

A parameter update would have been poorly placed. It might teach an agent to
avoid the tool or reconstruct the dropped field, while other callers remain
exposed. A memory warning would depend on retrieval. The regression check blocks a known bad output; the repaired tool changes the
mechanism. Both are needed for the claimed repair, and neither establishes
correctness outside the checked scope.

Months later the manifest format removes the optional field. The old test now
blocks a valid migration. Material change invalidates its qualification. The
test is retired with a record of why it once existed, and the tool admits the
new format through a fresh versioned contract.

The two paths begin with equal green outcomes and end with different durable
structures. That difference is the work of learning.

## Deoptimization and Retirement

Adaptive systems need a way to become less committed. Deoptimization removes
or narrows structure that no longer earns its carrying cost.

Every persistent lesson consumes something: context, storage, validation,
monitoring, human review, compatibility work, rollback preparation, or
organizational flexibility. Old rules can conflict with new ones. Defensive
tests can freeze obsolete interfaces. Memories can crowd retrieval. Parameters
can retain behavior after its evidence expires.

Retirement conditions should be designed with the original commitment. They
may include date, version change, population drift, contradictory evidence,
replacement by a stronger locus, repeated non-use, or failure to reproduce.
Expiry should usually trigger review, not silent deletion, when descendants or
rights are involved.

Deoptimization preserves permitted decision history while withdrawing or
narrowing current use. Earlier effects and learned influence may persist, and
required payload deletion can limit historical reconstruction. This distinction supports accountability without forcing the system to
carry every past belief forever.

A mature learner measures deletion and recovery as first-class capabilities.
It should be able to answer not only how quickly a lesson entered operation, but
how completely it can be challenged, narrowed, and withdrawn.

## Failure Modes

**Outcome worship.** A score or success is stored as its own explanation.

**First-story lock-in.** The earliest causal account gains persistence before
alternatives are recorded.

**Parameter reflex.** Every useful signal becomes a training example even when
a memory, test, tool repair, or environmental change fits better.

**Memory landfill.** Temporary warnings remain active after stronger controls
replace them.

**Cross-locus duplication.** The same rule persists in prompts, memory,
procedures, tools, and weights with no authority order.

**Evaluator capture.** The learner improves the judge that then approves the
learner.

**Reward ontology.** Proxy improvement is reported as objective improvement.

**Counterfactual hindsight.** Alternatives invented after an outcome are used
to assign regret as if they were available before it.

**Generalization by adjective.** A result is called robust or scalable without
a prospective population and failure criterion.

**Success-only memory.** Failed forecasts and update attempts disappear from
the denominator.

**Rollback theater.** One artifact is restored while descendant effects remain.

**Forgetting by suppression.** A model stops emitting an answer under familiar
prompts and the system claims deletion or privacy.

**Deletion by inventory.** Removing known files is treated as proof that no
copy, derivative, or influence remains.

**Scientific self-confirmation.** One automated pipeline proposes, tests,
selects, and validates a hypothesis through shared dependencies.

**Permanent learning.** No review, expiry, or retirement condition accompanies
the update.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline is not a self-modifying system with elaborate central
adjudication. It is a competent human-reviewed process with versioned memory,
ordinary tests, reproducible training, explicit model releases, data lineage,
and deletion tickets.

Local owners know their surfaces. A tool maintainer can often place a fix faster
than a general persistence service. Mature machine-learning platforms already
provide experiment tracking, checkpointing, canaries, and rollback. Scientific
teams already use preregistration and independent replication when incentives
permit.

The adaptive commit boundary earns its cost only if it improves decisions
across those surfaces. It should be compared on placement accuracy, time to
useful correction, transfer, collateral change, retained capability, deletion,
recovery, lifecycle cost, human comprehension, and resistance to manipulated
feedback.

If fixed-locus or human-reviewed policies match those outcomes at lower cost,
the boundary should contract. Shared contracts and descendant records may still
be useful without a general adjudicator.

## What the Current Work Establishes

The central Adjudicated Persistence architecture is presently an argument and
research program. The repository does not contain a running cross-surface
adjudicator, qualifier, deoptimizer, or descendant-revocation system. Five proof
targets and five experimental suites are planned, not implemented or run. The
chapter therefore does not establish that persistence adjudication improves
placement, transfer, deletion, recovery, or safety.

[Learning Theory](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/learning-theory-generalization-and-scaling-science.html)
checks a six-transition authored forecast lifecycle, finite attempt and
alternative custody, exact repair dispositions, and a rejecting benchmark
bridge. Its countermodels expose what summaries cannot determine. These are
record properties, not natural generalization, transfer, emergence, or scaling.

[Policy Optimization](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/policy-optimization-and-learning-from-feedback.html)
checks a synthetic six-sample, five-candidate lease and finite lifecycle routes.
Its router-policy fixture distinguishes reward from target, retains holdouts
and contamination controls, and exercises dry-run rollback. No optimizer,
model, natural preference dataset, live canary, causal improvement, or rollback
efficacy was tested. Its support effect is none.

[Data Engines](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/data-engines-continual-learning-and-unlearning.html)
checks an authored composed lifecycle and a full-state bridge separating
checkpoint authority, local restoration, and unlearning claims. Bounded local
campaigns restore tracked state and remove a named cohort from specified
surfaces, but they do not
establish deletion, forgetting, influence removal, privacy, rights compliance,
or external erasure. Matching a declared inventory is not open-world closure.

[Scientific Discovery](https://corbensorenson.github.io/asi-stack-book/chapters/scientific-discovery-and-experimental-governance.html)
checks an eight-transition authored lifecycle, attempt and confirmatory
custody, exact repair, and rejecting evidence consumers. It establishes finite
record and routing properties, not causal discovery, independent replication,
safety, support, release, or an external effect. The canonical owners retain
the exact theorem, route, fixture, mutation, and bounded-campaign inventories.

Together these artifacts establish finite control semantics around
forecasting, update leases, data-state recovery, and scientific records. They
do not establish the integrated adaptive commit boundary described in this
unit, and they do not demonstrate a superior continual-learning system.

## From Minimum Persistence to a Mature Learning System

A minimum implementation can use the two repository incidents. Build an
experience packet for each, record causal alternatives, and create candidate
lessons. Require an adjudicator that can choose among no change, temporary
context, dated memory, procedure, and typed tool test. It must state why the
chosen locus is smaller than the rejected alternatives.

Qualify both lessons prospectively. Inject stale evidence, evaluator conflict,
scope widening, missing authority, failed rollback, and material change. Verify
that the memory entry expires and that the tool test retires when the format
changes. Preserve descendants and non-claims.

The next stage adds policy updates, full-state checkpoints, data lineage, and
separate unlearning claims. Compare adjudicated placement with memory-only,
parameter-only, rule-based local, and human-review baselines. Measure whole-
lifecycle cost, not only immediate task success.

Natural campaigns should span different kinds of learning: software incidents,
user feedback, model adaptation, evaluator revision, data deletion, and
scientific hypothesis testing. Independent reviewers should judge causal
accounts and placement without seeing the architecture label. Failed campaigns
remain in the denominator.

A mature system would treat every durable adaptation as a typed, leased,
challengeable commitment. It would choose among loci, compile qualification
obligations from commitment, preserve prospective forecasts, detect proxy-
target divergence, trace descendants, restore complete state, and retire stale
structure. No component would gain durable influence merely by producing its
own evidence.

## The Strongest Objection

Persistence adjudication risks bureaucracy, analysis paralysis, centralized
power and one ontology imposed on unlike domains. A shared gate can itself
become a manipulation target.

That objection has teeth. Most low-risk local changes should remain cheap.
Standing policies can authorize reversible memory writes and tool tests within
bounded scopes. Human review may outperform automated causal adjudication for
rare, ambiguous changes. Domain owners should retain authority over meanings
that a generic service cannot infer.

The architecture should therefore scale review with commitment. It should
federate authority, expose dissent, and permit consumers to use only the
contracts they need. Its purpose is not to maximize process. It is to prevent a
success signal from silently becoming an irreversible cross-system change.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The adaptive commit boundary should narrow or be retired if competent fixed-
locus policies or human review match its placement quality, transfer,
retention, deletion, recovery, and safety at lower lifecycle cost.

Support would require prospective natural campaigns with matched resources,
independent causal and placement assessment, real competing baselines,
cross-domain transfer, adversarial feedback, long-horizon forgetting and
deoptimization, descendant-aware deletion, full-state recovery, and external
reproduction. The studies must report abstentions, failed updates, human labor,
compute, latency, and residual harm.

No finite Lean model can establish those empirical effects. Formal work can
prove that authored records obey stated commitment and revocation rules; it
cannot prove that the chosen lesson is true, that the evaluator is legitimate,
or that every descendant has been erased.

## What This Establishes

Experience, feedback, and reward are inputs to learning, not permission to
change durable structure. A candidate lesson needs identity, causal alternatives,
scope, lineage, and a lifecycle.

Context, memory, procedure, tool, parameter, evaluator, environment, and
institution are different persistence loci. The least consequential sufficient
locus should be preferred, with evidence matched to reach, duration, authority,
and reversibility.

Generalization is a prospective forecast. Policy updates are leased candidates.
Continual learning requires full-state and descendant custody. Unlearning is a
family of bounded claims, not a synonym for suppression or file deletion.
Scientific discovery remains governed revision rather than self-certifying
output.

The repository has finite formal and executable controls for several pieces of
this lifecycle. It does not yet implement or validate the integrated
adjudicator.

A candidate lesson still cannot decide whether it is safe to promote. Unit 22
assembles adversarial evaluation, readiness thresholds, residual custody, and a
structured assurance case for that decision.
